doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Playing 'Portrait of George' at Carnegie Hall in a janitor's closet
summary: With the Cincinnati Pops and Erich Kunzel, he had to play off stage and ended up in a janitor's closet, which relieved his nerves.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: was this thing called “Portrait of George.” And I didn’t record it. The guy that did record it was one of the greatest trumpet players I ever heard in my life and he lived only in Cincinnati, never left there. And he died young. Somebody shot him in a bar. But this guy was the most amazing player I ever heard. So I was channeling my Frank Brown you know but I said well I’m pretty nervous about this. And the first thing that happens in this piece, “Portrait of George,” it’s George Gershwin, three tunes. And it featured a trombone, a sax, and a trumpet. They were all the three best people in Cincinnati you know, at the time that that recording was done. And of course he was gone, so the other two guys were there and me. And so I’m getting ready to play and the first thing that happens [scats] to the high F. All alone. In Carnegie Hall. And I played off stage. So I was saying oh crap there is no off stage here in Carnegie Hall. There is none. There’s the one stage but it was on the other side of the stage. On my side there just was this door. And Erich Kunzel was conducting and he saw me standing there and he goes, “What are you doing? You’ve got to get off stage.” I said, “Well there isn’t any off-stage.” “There’s a door over there. Go open the door.” I opened the door and it was the janitor’s closet. And in there there’s this old lectern that, you know looked like it had been dented a thousand times from banging into something. And then there was the custodian’s mop barrel filled with water and smelly mops. So I go in there and I started laughing. I said I’m in Carnegie Hall janitor’s office. And Kunzel’s going, “What are you doing in there?” Because he wanted me to start playing because, you know we only had a little dress rehearsal in there and then we had to play the concert that night. I said, “Oh I’m getting ready, Erich, I have to set the music stand.” Because I didn’t bring my music stand in there. There wasn’t any music stand. And so that laugh sort of changed my life. Because I realized hell I’m in a janitor’s closet, what’s the difference between playing in a janitor’s closet and on stage? It doesn’t make any difference. And so it was an enlightening moment at the right time for me. It was just the right time for it. You know my grandparents were out there and you know stuff, and my mom and dad and my aunts and uncles. All the Italian — the whole Italian crew was there. So it was fun.
